title: Quantifying AI data center nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from space
content:
Physics > Atmospheric and Oceanic Physics
  [Submitted on 23 Aug 2026]
    Title:Quantifying AI data center nitrogen oxide (NO$_x$) emissions from space
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:AI data center power demand is spurring rapid deployment of on- and near-site natural gas turbines. Nitrogen oxide (NO$_x$) pollution from this equipment is a growing concern but has not previously been quantified with atmospheric observations. Here we demonstrate space-based detection and quantification of NO$_x$ emissions from the SpaceXAI Colossus 2 power plant in Southaven, Mississippi. Using observations from the geostationary TEMPO satellite instrument, we detect a strong increase in local mean NO$_2$ column concentrations after the plant began operations in late 2025. We then use TEMPO to estimate two-week-average NO$_x$ source rates from August 2025 to mid-August 2026, calibrating against continuous emission monitoring system (CEMS) data from US power plants. TEMPO first detected NO$_x$ emissions in December 2025 at 460$\pm$180 kg h$^{-1}$. We find that emissions increased through August 2026, averaging 730$\pm$185 kg h$^{-1}$ after February 2026, roughly 16 times higher than expected from the facility's March 2026 permit for 41 turbines operating under best available control technology (BACT) requirements ($\sim$47 kg h$^{-1}$). Emissions at the expected level would be undetectable by our TEMPO analysis.

report.summary: Satellite data show AI data center turbines emit 16 times more NOx than permitted, revealing a major environmental monitoring gap.
report.background: AI data centers require enormous, round-the-clock electricity, leading to rapid deployment of natural gas turbines on or near facilities. These turbines produce nitrogen oxides (NOx), pollutants linked to smog, acid rain, and respiratory illness, but their emissions had not previously been independently measured from space. This study uses NASA's geostationary TEMPO satellite to detect and quantify NOx from the SpaceXAI Colossus 2 power plant in Southaven, Mississippi. After the plant began operations in late 2025, the satellite observed a strong increase in local NO2 columns. Calibrating against continuous emission monitoring systems from U.S. power plants, the researchers estimated emissions averaged 730 kg/h after February 2026—about 16 times higher than the facility's March 2026 permit levels under best available control technology. The work highlights both the environmental cost of AI infrastructure and the value of satellite monitoring for verifying compliance.
key_points: Using NASA's TEMPO geostationary satellite, researchers detected a clear increase in NO2 columns over the SpaceXAI Colossus 2 facility in Southaven, Mississippi after it began operating in late 2025. This marks the first space-based detection of NOx emissions specifically attributed to AI data center power generation.

Calibrating satellite observations against continuous emission monitoring systems at US power plants, the team estimated two-week-average NOx source rates. Emissions were first detected December 2025 at 460±180 kg/h and rose to an average of 730±185 kg/h after February 2026, showing a clear upward trend.

The measured emissions are roughly 16 times higher than the facility's March 2026 permit level of ~47 kg/h for 41 turbines under best available control technology. This large discrepancy suggests actual operating conditions or control equipment performance differ substantially from permit assumptions.

At permitted levels, the emissions would be undetectable by this TEMPO analysis, meaning satellite methods only catch major exceedances. This highlights the need for more sensitive monitoring tools, careful permit design, and perhaps continuous on-site monitoring to ensure compliance and protect local air quality.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a wake-up call: the current buildout of behind-the-meter gas turbines may be polluting far more than permitted, creating regulatory and reputational risk. Developers should invest in best available control technologies, continuous monitoring, and cleaner power sources to avoid penalties. For regular users, the effects are local—communities near data centers may face increased smog, respiratory problems, and environmental injustice. For policymakers, satellite remote sensing offers a powerful way to verify emissions, complementing ground-based CEMS. The finding also suggests permits may need updating as AI loads grow quickly.
report.tools: Readers can explore NASA TEMPO data via the NASA Earthdata portal and the Harvard TEMPO mission site. For analysis, open-source Python packages such as xarray, satpy, and matplotlib are useful. EPA's Clean Air Markets Division provides public CEMS data for comparison. Google Earth Engine may also host TEMPO NO2 products for mapping and time series.
